description.s: View code changes now live-reload (rendering system watches
and bypasses selector filtering when the view itself changed). But library changes still require a page refresh — updating a library item doesn't trigger re-renders of views that use it.
Hob views re-evaluate from scratch on each render. Every

call executes again, so if the module cache is invalidated, the next render automatically picks up new library code. In JS, views capture library exports in closures at load time — even after cache invalidation, existing closures still hold old references.
The Hob interpreter controls execution, so

calls during eval can be intercepted to build a dependency graph: "this render instance depends on libraries X, Y, Z." When library X is updated, the system knows exactly which instances to re-render. This is the same pattern as
— the interpreter already tracks which items a render depends on.
registers the library's item ID as a dependency on the current render instance (analogous to how
for a library, look up dependent instances and schedule re-renders
Invalidate the module cache entry for that library so re-eval gets fresh code
Bypass selector filtering for library changes (same as view changes)

Should library dependencies be tracked per-instance (like selectors) or globally? Per-instance is more precise but global may be fine in practice — libraries rarely change, and when they do you probably want everything using them to refresh.

Harder for JS views because closures capture library exports at module load time. Even with cache invalidation, existing JS view code still references old exports. Full re-render (re-evaluating the JS module from scratch) would be needed, which is effectively what Hob already does naturally.

Hob should be the obvious choice for

user-programming within Hobson. There should be no reason to choose JS except for familiarity. Hob — and its integration with Hobson (item references, code-as-data, structural editing, queryable AST) — should be better than JS for most things, and as good for the rest.

This reframes the remaining work. The goal is not "add enough primitives to convert the remaining views" — it's to make Hob genuinely superior for Hobson programming. Every primitive should be designed so that Hob is what you'd choose even if you knew JS perfectly.

description.s: Mobile-friendly text editor for Hob expressions. Renders the compact JSON AST via hob-interpreter.prettyPrintAll, edits as plain text in a textarea, and parses back via hob-interpreter.readAll on every input (debounced 200ms). Parse errors are shown inline in a red banner; successful parses fire onChange with the new AST. A Format button reformats the current text. Readonly mode renders a pre block.
Designed for simple reminder expressions. :doc nodes round-trip as (:doc ...) lists — noisy but correct. No autocomplete, no syntax highlighting, no internal Save button.

Hob language interpreter — A Lisp dialect for the Hobson item system.

## Public API

```javascript
// Full interpreter with item operations
const hob = await api.require('hob-interpreter');
const interp = hob.createInterpreter(api);
const result = await interp.eval('(+ 1 2)'); // => 3

// Direct access for testing
const ast = hob.read('(+ 1 2)');
const result = await hob.evaluate(ast, env);
const str = hob.prStr(result);
```

## Language Features

- **Literals:** numbers, strings, booleans, nil, keywords, item refs (@name)
- **Collections:** vectors `[1 2 3]`, maps `{:a 1}`, lists `(1 2 3)`
- **Special forms:** def, fn, let, if, do, quote, quasiquote, loop/recur, try/catch/throw, defmacro, plet
- **Macros:** defn, when, when-let, cond, ->, ->>, for, and, or
- **Destructuring:** vector `[a b & rest]`, map `{:keys [a b] :or {b 10} :as m}`
- **Multi-arity functions:** `(fn ([x] ...) ([x y] ...))`
- **Atoms:** atom, deref, swap!, reset!
- **Concurrency:** auto-parallel let, plet, pmap
- **Anonymous fn shorthand:** `#(+ %1 %2)`
- **Standard library:** arithmetic, strings, collections, predicates, I/O
- **Item operations:** get-item, set-item!, delete-item!, get-all, find-items
- **REPL integration:** Use `:hob` or `:h` prefix in the REPL

Item search functionality used throughout Hobson. Provides both a search function and a reusable search UI widget. All search evaluates on Enter (not on every keystroke).
Two modes: filter syntax (text-based) and Hob expressions.

# Text search
meeting notes              # matches items containing both words

# Type filter
type:note                  # exact type match by name or ID
type:code+                 # type or subtypes (inherited)
type:note,task             # OR: note or task

# Tag filter
tag:todo                   # has tag
tag:todo,urgent            # OR: has todo OR urgent
tag:todo tag:urgent        # AND: has both
#todo                      # shorthand for tag:todo

# Negation
-type:renderer             # exclude type
-tag:archived              # exclude tag
-keyword                   # exclude text

# Field-specific
name:my-lib                # search name field
title:"quoted phrase"      # quoted phrase

# Sort
sort:modified               # most recent first
sort:created                # newest first
sort:name                   # alphabetical
When the query starts with (, it is evaluated as a Hob expression. A macro automatically inserts the item argument into known predicates and wraps the result in a filter/sort pipeline.

# Predicate only (default sort: most recent first)
(type? "note")
(tagged? "todo")
(and (type? "note") (tagged? "todo"))
(name? "kernel")
(text? "meeting notes")

# With sort
(type? "note") (sort :name :asc)
(tagged? "todo") (sort :created)

# Sort only (all items)
(sort :modified)

# Ad-hoc expressions (use i for the item)
(> (.-modified i) 1710000000000)

;;; --- JavaScript ---
(defn render [item api]
  (def attachments (or (:attachments item) []))
  (def default-view-id "a1b2c3d4-e5f6-4a7b-8c9d-0e1f2a3b4c5d")
  [:div.sortable-list-view {:style "display: flex; flex-direction: column; height: 100%; background: var(--color-bg-surface-alt);"}

    [:div.sortable-list-items {:style "flex: 1; overflow-y: auto; padding-left: 2px; padding-top: 4px; padding-bottom: 10px; padding-right: 2px;"
                               :sortable {:handle ".drag-handle"
                                          :on-reorder (fn [from to]
                                                        (reorder-attachments!
                                                          from
                                                          to))}}
      (if
        (seq attachments)
        (for [child (seq attachments)]
          (let [child-id (if (string? child) child (:id child))
                view-id (or (get-in child [:view :type]) default-view-id)]
            [:div.sortable-list-item {:data-item-id child-id

                                      :data-sort-key child-id
                                      :style "display: flex; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 4px;"}

content.code:
(defn render [item api]
  (def search item)
  (def target-container (get-in search [:content :target_container]))
  (def attachments (or (:attachments search) []))
  (def starred-ids (or (get-in search [:content :starredIds]) []))
  (def recent-ids (or (get-in search [:content :recentIds]) []))
  (def default-view-id "d4e5f6a7-b8c9-4d0e-a1b2-c3d4e5f6a7b8")
  (def saved-ast (get-in search [:content :currentAst]))
  (def is-default (nil? saved-ast))
  (def default-ast (parse-hob! "(text? \"\")"))
  (def pending-ast (atom (or saved-ast default-ast)))
  (def is-modal (= (get-parent-id) "88888888-0000-0000-0000-000000000000"))

  (def error-div (js/document.createElement "div"))
  (dom-set! (dom-get error-div :style) :cssText "display: none; margin-bottom: 16px; padding: 10px 14px; border: 1px solid var(--color-error, #c00); border-radius: var(--border-radius); color: var(--color-error, #c00); font-family: monospace; font-size: 0.875rem; white-space: pre-wrap;")

  (defn do-submit [ast]
    (dom-set! error-div :textContent "")
    (dom-set! (dom-get error-div :style) :display "none")
    (try
      (let [matches (eval-search-ast! ast)
            new-atts (vec (map (fn [m] {:id (:id m)}) matches))
            fresh (get-item (:id item))]
        (set-item!
          (->
            fresh
            (assoc :attachments new-atts)
            (assoc-in [:content :currentAst] ast)
            (assoc :modified (now)))))
      (catch e
        (dom-set! error-div :textContent (str e))
        (dom-set! (dom-get error-div :style) :display "block"))))

  (def struct-ed (require "field-view-hob-structural"))
  (def editor-el
    (let [el (.render struct-ed
      (deref pending-ast)
      {:compact true
       :autoFocus is-modal
       :onChange (fn [new-ast] (reset! pending-ast new-ast))
       :onSubmit do-submit}
      api)]
      (dom-set! el :id (str "search-editor-" (now)))
      el))

  (defn render-group [ids]
    (for [id ids]
      [:render-child {:item id
                      :view default-view-id
                      :open-in (or target-container (get-parent-id))
                      :data-sort-key id}]))

  [:div.item-search-view {:style "width: 100%; max-width: 800px; margin: 0 auto; padding: 20px; box-sizing: border-box;"}

    [:div {:style "margin-bottom: 20px; padding-bottom: 15px; border-bottom: 2px solid var(--color-border-light);"}
      [:h2 {:style "margin: 0; font-size: 1.25rem;"}
        (or (:name search) "Search")]]

    [:div {:style "display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 8px; margin-bottom: 4px;"}
      [:div {:style "flex: 1; min-width: 0;"}
        editor-el]
      [:button
        {:style "padding: 6px 14px; background: var(--color-primary); color: white; border: none; border-radius: var(--border-radius); cursor: pointer; font-size: 0.875rem; white-space: nowrap; flex-shrink: 0;"
         :onClick (fn [] (do-submit (deref pending-ast)))}
        "Search"]]

    [:div {:style "margin-bottom: 16px; font-size: 0.75rem; color: var(--color-text-secondary);"}
      "Ctrl+Enter or tap Search  ·  e.g. (type? \"note\")  (tagged? \"todo\")  (sort :modified)"]

    error-div

    (if
      is-default
      [:div
        (when (seq recent-ids)
          [:details {:open true :style "margin-bottom: 12px;"}
            [:summary {:style "font-size: 0.875rem; color: var(--color-text-secondary); font-weight: 500; cursor: pointer; padding: 4px 0; margin-bottom: 8px;"}
              "Recent"]
            (render-group recent-ids)])
        (when (seq starred-ids)
          [:details {:open true :style "margin-bottom: 12px;"}
            [:summary {:style "font-size: 0.875rem; color: var(--color-text-secondary); font-weight: 500; cursor: pointer; list-style: none; padding: 4px 0; margin-bottom: 8px;"}
              "★ Starred"]
            (render-group starred-ids)])
        (when (and (empty? starred-ids) (empty? recent-ids))
          [:div {:style "padding: 40px; text-align: center; color: var(--color-border-dark); font-style: italic;"}
            "Tap Search or press Ctrl+Enter to run the query"])]
      (if
        (empty? attachments)
        [:div {:style "text-align: center; padding: 40px;"}
          [:div {:style "color: var(--color-text-secondary);"} "No items found"]]
        [:div
          [:div {:style "margin-bottom: 15px; font-size: 0.875rem; color: var(--color-text-secondary); font-weight: 500;"}
            (str "Found " (count attachments) " item" (if (= (count attachments) 1) "" "s"))]
          (for [att attachments]
            (let [child-id (if (map? att) (:id att) att)
                  view-id (or (get-in att [:view :type]) default-view-id)]
              [:render-child {:item child-id
                              :view view-id
                              :open-in (or target-container (get-parent-id))
                              :data-sort-key child-id}]))]))])

Hobson draws from several foundational ideas in interactive computing, personal information management, and live programming environments. Understanding these influences helps explain why the system works the way it does.
describes twelve attributes that make interactive applications feel natural and empowering. Hobson aspires to embody all of them.
Saving an item re-renders it immediately
Items are granular; edits are atomic
Links and context menus reveal pathways
The tool disappears; you touch the material
Everything is an item; no hidden layers
Edit code items while system runs
Actions are reversible, system doesn't break
Safe mode, type validation, error capture
Source and runtime are the same
Hobson can render and edit itself
See data flow in real time

pioneered the idea that the entire development environment--objects, classes, methods, and state--lives in a persistent "image" rather than external files. When you close Smalltalk, you save the image; when you reopen it, everything is exactly as you left it.
: All items persist in the browser's IndexedDB
: Code items are evaluated directly from storage
: Close the tab, reopen it, and your workspace remains
: Edit a kernel module, reload, and changes take effect
Unlike Smalltalk, Hobson stores code as text (ES modules) rather than bytecode, enabling inspection and editing with standard tools.

The original system had renderers (display) and editors (modify) as separate item types. A single view concept replaced this because most views naturally want per-field mode control (some fields readonly, others editable), not all-or-nothing.

Views are items, not embedded in type definitions. This means you can add a new view without modifying the type, users can create alternative views, and views are inspectable and modifiable like everything else.

Hob views produce a complete DOM tree on every render. Morphdom diffs the new tree against the existing DOM and patches only what changed, preserving scroll positions, form inputs, and focus. Old event handlers are retained (they have correct refs to the kept DOM elements).

description.s: Tag for implementation patterns — recipes for writing correct Hobson code.
Defines the type of items used to view history.

When switching the root workspace from spatial-canvas-view to sortable-list-view, child items render with their spatial-canvas-specific view overrides (e.g. History Viewer renders as item-history-view instead of a compact inline card). The sortable-list-view reads the attachment's view.type and uses it, but that view.type was set by/for the spatial canvas.
The attachment spec carries three unrelated concerns in one object:
Compositional relationship — this item is a child of this parent (id)
Per-context view preference — how to render this child in this parent (view.type)
View-specific state — spatial positioning, background layers, previous view history (x, y, innerView, etc.)

Concern 3 is the problem. Spatial canvas positioning and innerView history are specific to a particular parent view, but stored on the shared attachment entry where every parent view sees them. A sortable list cannot distinguish "the user wants this child rendered as item-history-view everywhere" from "the spatial canvas was using this view with these coordinates".
A History Viewer attachment in a workspace:
The view.type, innerView, and spatial fields are all spatial-canvas-specific, but the sortable list reads view.type and renders item-history-view instead of its default card view.

The "View As..." context menu handler (context-menu-lib) sets view.type to the newly selected view, then saves the previously-rendered view as innerView. This was designed for spatial-canvas-view's full-bleed background feature. It means the attachment accumulates view-switching history as a side effect.

Commit 75f39a8 removed the child view snapshot/restore mechanism from setAttachmentView. That code used to save all child view configs into savedViewStates on switch and clear them, restoring when switching back. It was removed to "stop mutating shared item data on view switch" (sync safety concern). The result is that spatial-canvas view state now persists across parent view switches.
— Always use the default card view. Simple, but the sortable list can never have per-child view overrides.
— Save child view configs in savedViewStates on switch, clear them, restore on switch-back. Restores pre-75f39a8 behaviour but conflicts with the sync-safety intent.
C. Scope view state per parent view

— Store child view overrides (and spatial positioning) in a per-parent-view map rather than directly on the attachment. Each parent view gets its own namespace. This is the architecturally clean solution but a larger change.
D. Heuristic: ignore view.type if spatial fields present
— If the view config has x/y/width/height, treat it as spatial-canvas-specific. Fragile coupling between views.

The deeper question is whether the attachment spec should carry view-specific state at all, or whether view state should be scoped to the view that created it. This affects spatial positioning, view overrides, innerView history, and potentially future per-view state like scroll position or collapse state.

name: Attachment view state is not scoped to parent view

The kernel is Hobson's minimal runtime—the smallest possible core that enables everything else to be built as items.

principle: it provides only what cannot be implemented as userland items. Everything else—views, editors, error handling, search—lives outside the kernel as regular items that can be inspected, modified, or replaced.

Hobson embodies the \"always on\" principle from Conway's Humane Dozen. The app runs continuously (like Smalltalk) — no start/stop cycle. Modifying a code item changes running behavior immediately.

The Silent Update pattern solves a fundamental tension in Hobson: saving data to the database normally triggers a re-render, but during user interactions like dragging, re-rendering destroys the DOM and breaks the interaction mid-flight.
Hobson's reactive rendering means any call to

When a re-render is necessary (adding/removing attachments, content changes), the DOM is rebuilt from scratch. This destroys scroll positions, focus state, and other transient DOM state. The Scroll State Preservation pattern saves and restores this state across re-renders.

With morphdom now used for efficient DOM diffing in Hob views, full DOM replacement is less common. Morphdom patches the existing DOM in place, preserving scroll positions and focus state automatically. This pattern is primarily relevant for JS views that still do full DOM replacement, and for the spatial canvas container view.
Everything the user was looking at — scroll position within windows, which element had focus, text selections — is lost.

Hobson's module system caches evaluated code items for performance. Cache invalidation is event-driven — when an item is updated, its cache entry is deleted so the next

A Hob view pattern for building interactive UIs with local state that update efficiently without triggering kernel re-renders.

Hobson's rendering system re-evaluates a view's entire Hob code to produce a new DOM tree, then uses morphdom to diff it against the existing DOM. This works well for data-driven views, but is expensive and lossy for views with rich local state:
: Re-evaluation means re-querying all items from the database, rebuilding all data structures, and re-running all logic — even if only one tab changed.
: Even with morphdom diffing, a full re-render resets local state that lives outside the DOM: atom values, scroll positions in sibling panels, text in filter inputs, focus state.
: If the view uses atoms for local state (e.g. which tab is selected), and atom mutations trigger re-renders, the view re-renders itself infinitely.
The Solution: Build Once, Update Surgically
Split the view into two phases:
to create a stable outer DOM structure with named refs. This runs once, at initial evaluation.
to replace the children of specific ref'd containers. Call these imperatively when local state changes.

;; Phase 1: Stable skeleton (runs once)
(let [state (atom "tab-a")
      [root refs] (hiccup->dom+
        [:div {}
          [:div {:ref :tabs}]
          [:div {:ref :content}]])
      tabs-el (:tabs refs)
      content-el (:content refs)

      ;; Phase 2: Builder functions
      build-tabs! (fn []
        (dom-set-content! tabs-el
          (for [t ["tab-a" "tab-b"]]
            [:div {:style (if (= t (deref state)) "font-weight:bold" "")
                   :on-click (fn [e]
                               (reset! state t)
                               (build-tabs!)
                               (build-content!))}
              t])))
      build-content! (fn []
        (dom-set-content! content-el
          [:div {} (str "Showing: " (deref state))]))]

  ;; Initial render
  (build-tabs!)
  (build-content!)
  root)
Morphdom is the kernel's tool for diffing between full re-renders. It operates at the wrong level for intra-view updates:
Re-evaluate all Hob code, re-query DB

doesn't diff — it clears and replaces children of a specific container. This is efficient because each builder only touches a small subtree, and sibling containers (with their scroll positions, input values, etc.) are untouched.
Because builder functions often call each other (clicking a tab rebuilds both the tab bar and the content), and Hob's
bindings are sequential, use atoms for forward declaration:

(let [build-tabs!    (atom nil)
      build-content! (atom nil)

      _ (reset! build-tabs!
          (fn [] ... ((deref build-content!)) ...))

      _ (reset! build-content!
          (fn [] ...))
  ...)

If this mechanism breaks, the symptom is an infinite re-render loop: atom reset triggers re-render, re-render re-creates atoms, which triggers another re-render.

:h 42              ;; number
:h 3.14            ;; number (all numbers are doubles)
:h "hello"         ;; string
:h true            ;; boolean
:h false           ;; boolean

:h "line one\nline two"    ;; string with newline

Nesting works naturally — inner expressions evaluate first:

:h (not false)         ;; => true
:h (not nil)           ;; => true
:h (not 0)            ;; => false  (0 is truthy!)

:h (and true true)     ;; => true
:h (and true false)    ;; => false
:h (and nil "hello")   ;; => nil  (stops at first falsy)
:h (or false nil 42)   ;; => 42   (returns first truthy)
:h (or false nil)      ;; => nil   (all falsy)

:h (let [name "Alice" age 30] (str name " is " age " years old"))
;; => "Alice is 30 years old"

hob('(def x 42)')

Multi-expression body — last expression is the return value:

hob(`(defn greet [name]

A function can have different bodies for different argument counts:

:h (do
     (defn add
       ([x] x)
       ([x y] (+ x y))
       ([x y z] (+ x y z)))
     [(add 1) (add 1 2) (add 1 2 3)])
;; => [1 3 6]
Keywords act as getter functions when used in function position:
This is one of Hob's most useful idioms.
. Functionally similar to vectors but used mainly in macro contexts:
These are the workhorses of Hob code:

;; map — transform each element
:h (map inc [1 2 3])               ;; => [2 3 4]
:h (map str/upper-case ["a" "b"])  ;; => ["A" "B"]

;; filter — keep elements matching predicate
:h (filter #(> % 3) [1 5 2 7 3])  ;; => [5 7]

;; reduce — fold a collection to a single value
:h (reduce + [1 2 3 4])            ;; => 10
:h (reduce + 100 [1 2 3])          ;; => 106 (with initial value)

;; some — find first truthy result
:h (some #(> % 3) [1 2 5 3])      ;; => true
:h (some #(> % 10) [1 2 3])       ;; => nil

;; every? — all elements satisfy predicate?
:h (every? #(> % 0) [1 2 3])      ;; => true
:h (every? #(> % 2) [1 2 3])      ;; => false

;; sort and sort-by
:h (sort [3 1 4 1 5])              ;; => [1 1 3 4 5]
:h (sort-by count ["bb" "a" "ccc"]) ;; => ["a" "bb" "ccc"]

;; distinct, reverse, take
:h (distinct [1 2 1 3 2])          ;; => [1 2 3]
:h (reverse [1 2 3])               ;; => [3 2 1]
:h (take 2 [10 20 30 40])          ;; => [10 20]

;; mapcat — map then flatten one level
:h (mapcat #(list % %) [1 2 3])    ;; => (1 1 2 2 3 3)

:h (if true "yes" "no")        ;; => "yes"
:h (if false "yes" "no")       ;; => "no"
:h (if nil "yes" "no")         ;; => "no"
:h (if nil "yes")              ;; => nil  (no else branch)
with no else branch, but allows multiple body expressions:
— bind and execute body only if the value is truthy:

:h (let [x 10
         y 20
         sum (+ x y)]
     (str "sum is " sum))
;; => "sum is 30"
Bindings are sequential — later bindings can reference earlier ones. Bindings are scoped to the let block.
Hob analyzes let bindings for dependencies. Independent bindings run concurrently:

;; x and y have no dependencies on each other — they evaluate in parallel.
;; z depends on both — it waits for them.
:h (let [x (do (log "computing x") 1)
         y (do (log "computing y") 2)
         z (+ x y)]
     z)
;; => 3
forces all bindings to evaluate concurrently, regardless of apparent dependencies:
Destructuring extracts values from collections directly in binding positions. It works in

:h (let [[a b c] [1 2 3]] (str a ", " b ", " c))
;; => "1, 2, 3"

;; Rest elements with &
:h (let [[head & tail] [1 2 3 4]] tail)
;; => (2 3 4)

;; Skip elements with _
:h (let [[_ second _] [1 2 3]] second)
;; => 2

;; :keys extracts keyword keys by name
:h (let [{:keys [name age]} {:name "Alice" :age 30}] (str name " is " age))
;; => "Alice is 30"

;; :strs extracts string keys
:h (let [{:strs [name]} {"name" "Bob"}] name)
;; => "Bob"

;; :or provides defaults
:h (let [{:keys [x y] :or {x 0 y 0}} {:x 5}] [x y])
;; => [5 0]

;; :as binds the whole map
:h (let [{:keys [name] :as person} {:name "Alice" :age 30}] [name person])
;; => ["Alice" {:name "Alice", :age 30}]

;; Direct key binding
:h (let [{city :city} {:city "NYC"}] city)
;; => "NYC"

:h (do
     (defn full-name [{:keys [first last]}]
       (str first " " last))
     (full-name {:first "Jane" :last "Doe"}))
;; => "Jane Doe"

:h (do
     (defn sum-pair [[a b]] (+ a b))
     (sum-pair [3 4]))
;; => 7
jumps back to the loop head with new values — this is tail recursion with no stack growth:

:h (loop [i 0 sum 0]
     (if (> i 10)
       sum
       (recur (inc i) (+ sum i))))
;; => 55  (sum of 0..10)

:h (do
     (defn factorial [n]
       (loop [i n acc 1]
         (if (<= i 1)
           acc
           (recur (dec i) (* acc i)))))
     (factorial 10))
;; => 3628800
iterates for side effects, returns nil:

:h (doseq [x [1 2 3]] (log (str "x = " x)))
;; logs: x = 1, x = 2, x = 3
;; => nil
Threading macros help avoid deeply nested function calls.

;; Without threading:
:h (str/upper-case (subs (str/trim "  hello world  ") 0 5))

;; With ->:
:h (-> "  hello world  " str/trim (subs 0 5) str/upper-case)
;; => "HELLO"
Atoms hold mutable state. They're the primary way to manage state in Hob views. Since atoms are stateful, use

hob('(def counter (atom 0))')
hob('(deref counter)')              ;; => 0
hob('(swap! counter inc)')          ;; => 1
hob('(swap! counter + 10)')         ;; => 11  (applies (+ current 10))
hob('(reset! counter 0)')           ;; => 0
hob('(deref counter)')              ;; => 0

hob('(def state (atom {:count 0 :items []}))')
hob('(swap! state update :count inc)')
hob('(swap! state update :items conj "new item")')
hob('(deref state)')
;; => {:count 1, :items ["new item"]}
In Hob views, atoms are automatically tracked for reactivity — when an atom that a view depends on changes, the view re-renders.

:h (try
     (/ 1 0)
     (catch e
       (str "Error: " e)))
;; => "Error: Division by zero"  (or similar)

:h (try
     (throw "something went wrong")
     (catch e
       (str "Caught: " e))
     (finally
       (log "cleanup runs always")))
;; => "Caught: something went wrong"

:h (do
     (defn positive! [n]
       (when (< n 0)
         (throw (str "Expected positive, got " n)))
       n)
     (try (positive! -3)
       (catch e (str "Oops: " e))))
;; => "Oops: Expected positive, got -3"

Design Approach: Separate Views, Not Responsive CSS

Pro: plays to Hobson's strengths (the view system already resolves which view for which context), clean code (no branching), independent iteration, phone UI can be radically different from desktop. Item search (Ctrl+K, Item Search view) supports filtering via a bespoke mini-language (type:, tag:, name:, title:, #shorthand, negation with -). Results always sort alphabetically. There is no way to sort by recency, filter by date, or compose queries beyond what the fixed syntax supports. Adding more capabilities means inventing more syntax — but we already have a programming language.
Proposal: Hob expressions as search predicates

When the search input starts with (, treat it as a Hob predicate expression. The search box macro-expands it into a complete Hob program that filters and sorts all items, then evaluates it in one interpreter call.

;; user writes
(and (type? "note") (tagged? "todo") (not (tagged? "done")))

;; expands to
(filter (fn [i]
  (and (type? i "note") (tagged? i "todo") (not (tagged? i "done"))))
  (get-all))
The search box applies a macro before evaluation. The macro:
Splits input on top-level expression boundaries. If there are two expressions and the second starts with (sort ...), extracts the sort directive
Walks the first (predicate) expression tree. For each call to a registered predicate function (type?, tagged?, etc.) that is missing its item argument, inserts i as the first argument
Wraps the result in (fn [i] ...) to produce a predicate function
Wraps in (filter pred (get-all)) and optionally (sort-by field :desc ...)

The macro needs a registry of predicate functions and their arities so it knows which calls are "missing" the item argument. This is a fixed, small set. For ad-hoc expressions, the user can reference i explicitly: (> (.-modified i) 1710000000000).
New stdlib or search-context functions. All take item as first argument.

(type? item "note")          ;; item.type matches type name or ID
(tagged? item "todo")        ;; item has tag by name or ID
(name? item "foo")           ;; item.name contains substring
(modified-after? item ts)    ;; item.modified > timestamp
(modified-before? item ts)   ;; item.modified < timestamp
(has-field? item :code)      ;; item.content has field
type? and tagged? resolve names to IDs (like the current search does), so users write human-readable names, not GUIDs.
All search — both plain text and Hob — evaluates on Enter, not on every keystroke. This is a change from the current debounce model, motivated by two problems:
The current debounce sometimes triggers mid-typing, and when results render the trailing keystrokes are lost — the user ends up with the wrong search text.
For Hob expressions, debounce or balanced-paren detection can't tell whether the user intends to add a (sort ...) expression after the predicate. Enter makes intent explicit.

The existing name:/type:/tag: syntax remains supported for quick interactive use. It is not replaced — it coexists. The Hob mode is for queries that go beyond what the mini-syntax can express.

If a balanced Hob expression fails to evaluate (typo, unknown symbol, wrong arity, etc.), display the Hob error message inline in the results area — where "Searching..." or results normally appear. No results are shown. This gives the user immediate feedback to fix their query.
— rejected because (type? "note") with a typo would silently become a text search for the literal string, returning random items that happen to contain those characters. Confusing.
— rejected because the user gets no signal about what went wrong. Showing the error is more helpful.
Benchmarked against 383 items (full database) and 2298 items (6x duplication):

383 items:
  JS filter:       0ms
  Hob per-item:   16ms  (JS loop calling Hob predicate per item)
  Hob all-in:    14ms  (entire filter inside Hob)

2298 items:
  JS filter:       0ms
  Hob per-item:   62ms  (JS↔Hob boundary crossing dominates)
  Hob all-in:      8ms  (single interpreter call)

Key finding: the JS↔Hob boundary crossing per item is the bottleneck, not Hob evaluation itself. Running the entire filter inside Hob (one boundary crossing) is fast — 8ms for 2298 items. The macro must therefore produce a complete Hob program, not a predicate function called from JS per item.

Sort is expressed as a second expression after the predicate. The search box splits the input on top-level expression boundaries: the first is the filter predicate, the second (optional) is the sort directive.

(type? "note") (sort :modified)           ;; find notes, most recent first
(tagged? "todo") (sort :name :asc)        ;; find todos, alphabetical
(and (type? "note") (tagged? "todo"))      ;; no sort — defaults to :modified :desc

This reads naturally left-to-right: "find items of this type, and sort them this way." Since evaluation is triggered by Enter (not balanced-paren detection), there is no ambiguity about whether the user intends to add a sort expression — Enter makes intent explicit.
If no sort is specified, default is :modified :desc (most recent first).

Time-based reminders on items, with native OS notifications on Android and desktop (both via Tauri).
Reminders are dedicated items, attached to their target items. Any item can have reminders via the attachment relationship. Multiple reminders per item are naturally supported.

Scheduling logic lives in userland. A userland library item wraps Tauri notification plugin calls. A boot-scan item runs on kernel:boot-complete to re-register alarms with the OS (handles reboots and process kills). The kernel has no knowledge of Tauri or notifications.

The native layer is a dumb translator — it receives timestamps and display text, schedules OS alarms, and shows notifications. All intelligence (recurrence, snooze, relative times) stays in userland Hob code.
Each reminder item contains a Hob expression that answers one question: "when next?" The expression evaluates to either a timestamp (schedule it) or nil (don't schedule).
— expression returns a fixed future timestamp; returns nil once dismissed.
— expression computes the next occurrence from now (e.g., next weekday at 9am).
One-shot vs recurring is a property of the expression, not a separate system concept.
The scheduling loop: evaluate → got a timestamp? → schedule with native layer → alarm fires → wake WebView → re-evaluate → repeat. Nil means stop.

If the WebView can't be woken after an alarm fires (e.g., OEM battery optimization killed the process), the next occurrence won't be scheduled until the user opens the app and boot-scan runs. This is expected behavior — same degradation as device reboots.

When a notification is tapped, deep-link to the reminder item (not the target). The reminder item provides dismiss/snooze/reschedule actions and navigation to the target via the attachment relationship.

name: JSON AST as Canonical Code Representation

description.s: Implemented (Feb 2026). Compact JSON AST is now the canonical storage and evaluation format. The field is
as originally proposed. Phase 1 (storage migration) and Phase 2 (direct evaluator dispatch) are both complete. See the implementation details below as historical context for the design decisions.
) as the canonical representation for code items. Comments are stored in a sibling property (
). A thin sugar layer and pretty printer provide s-expression syntax for human interaction, but neither is load-bearing — the system operates on JSON throughout.
Currently, Hob code is stored as text in
. The interpreter's reader parses this text into an internal AST (typed wrapper objects like
The system contains a ~200+ line recursive descent parser with escape handling, reader macros, and error recovery.
The parser is on the critical path — every code evaluation begins with a parse step.
Code is stored in a format (text) that is opaque to the rest of Hobson. Querying, indexing, or transforming code requires parsing it first.
The structural editor (if built) must parse on load and serialize on save, introducing round-trip fidelity concerns.
The Hobson philosophy is that everything is an item and items are JSON. Code stored as text is the one exception. This proposal eliminates that exception.
The representation maps Hob's types directly onto JSON's native types, tagging only what is ambiguous.

Symbols are the most common node type in code. By making them bare JSON strings (zero overhead), the representation is maximally compact for the common case. String literals are relatively rare in typical code and bear the small cost of a wrapper object. Keywords and item references are distinguished by prefix convention on the string, avoiding additional wrapper objects.
Vectors and maps require wrappers because JSON arrays are already used for lists. The wrapper key is a single character (
Quoting, quasiquoting, and unquoting are represented as explicit list forms rather than reader syntax:
This eliminates the need for reader macros in the representation. The sugar layer converts the shorthand syntax to these forms on input; the pretty printer converts back on output.
Comments are stored as a sibling property alongside the code, keyed by path into the AST.
A comment path is a dot-separated sequence of array indices locating a position in the AST:
— top-level comment on the entire expression
— before the element at index 3 of the root list
— before element at index 1 within the element at index 3
— trailing comment after the last element within element 3
They receive and return plain arrays with no comment wrappers to handle.
Comments are metadata about code, not code themselves.
Storing them separately reflects this truth.
A text sugar layer can extract and insert comments. A structural editor can display them alongside nodes. Neither requires special-casing in the AST.
When code is modified, comments with invalidated paths can be dropped or flagged. This mirrors text-based systems where refactoring discards comments on changed code.
Recursive descent, escape handling, reader macros, error recovery
S-expression text to JSON AST. UI-only, not on critical path.
JSON AST to s-expression text. UI-only.
Extract comments during sugar-layer parsing and produce
Simplifies. Receives and returns plain arrays. No AST node constructors needed.
Input goes through sugar layer before evaluation. Output goes through pretty printer.

replaces ~200+ lines of hand-written parser. It is built-in, battle-tested, and zero maintenance. The sugar layer exists only as a UI convenience and is not on any critical path — if it has a bug, the system still functions.

Code is stored in the same JSON format as every other item property. This is not a philosophical aspiration — it is literally true. The same tools that query, index, transform, and display item data work on code without any adaptation.

"Find all items that call function X" becomes a recursive walk over native JS arrays — no parse step required. Indexes can be built over the AST structure directly. Pattern matching against code structure is matching against plain JS values.
A future structural editor operates directly on the canonical representation. There is no parse-on-load / serialize-on-save cycle, no round-trip fidelity concerns. Every edit modifies the real data.
The evaluator dispatches on native JS types rather than wrapper objects. A
and a few property checks replaces a
Macros construct return values using array literals and object literals — standard JS. No AST constructor functions needed. A macro that transforms

when inspecting raw item JSON. Mitigated by the pretty printer for display and the sugar layer for input. In practice, users would rarely read raw JSON — they'd interact through the REPL, code editor, or structural editor.

The pretty printer makes all formatting decisions. Hand-formatting (aligning columns, grouping blank lines) is not preserved. This is consistent with modern auto-formatting (gofmt, Prettier) and is moot for a structural editor.

You cannot paste raw s-expression code from the web and have it work directly. The sugar layer handles conversion, but it's an extra step. In practice, Hob is not standard Scheme or Clojure — external code would need adaptation regardless.
Text-based errors report line and column. AST-based errors report paths like
. The pretty printer can reverse-map paths to rendered lines. A structural editor can highlight the node directly. Error quality depends on the evaluator's messages, not the representation.
cannot be represented in JSON. These are unlikely to appear as literals in Hob source code. If needed, they could be represented as symbols (
Conversion from text to JSON AST is fully automatable. A one-time migration tool would:
Parse using the existing Hob reader (with a small modification to capture comments and their positions rather than discarding them).
Map captured comment positions to AST paths.
The migration tool uses the existing parser one final time, then the parser can be retired. The tool is run once per item and then discarded.

This proposal is independent of but complementary to the structural editor design. The original design assumed Option B (parse text on load, serialize on save). With JSON AST as canonical, the structural editor instead operates directly on the stored representation — a strictly simpler architecture.
The sugar layer and pretty printer designed here serve double duty: they provide text-mode editing and REPL interaction now, and become the import/export layer for a structural editor later.
This change deepens the alignment between Hobson's design and its inspirations:
"Source" and "object" language representations become literally the same. Code items are JSON. Data items are JSON. There is one representation.
The AST is inspectable with the same tools as any item. No hidden text-parsing step stands between the user and their code's structure.

The system operates on live objects (JS arrays and primitives), not on text that must be parsed into objects. This is closer to how Smalltalk's image works — code exists as structured objects, not source files.
The representation is faithful to Lisp's "code is data" principle — more so than text, because the stored form
the data structure the evaluator consumes.
Everything is an item, queryable and linkable. Code was the last holdout stored as opaque text. This proposal closes that gap.

Hob is a small, interpreted Lisp dialect designed specifically for Hobson. It combines Lisp's implementation model — s-expressions, an interpreter, macros, homoiconicity — with Smalltalk's interaction philosophy: live inspection, graphical tools, and the principle that the tool and the material are made of the same stuff.
The language has three distinguishing properties:
Item references are a primitive type.
Reading an item is a language-level operation, not an API call. The runtime tracks dependencies automatically.
The AST is serialized into the item store, making code queryable, navigable, and modifiable with the same tools used for data.
The interpreter's eval loop is async JavaScript internally, but Hob code is written and experienced as synchronous. The concept of promises does not exist in the language.

The end state is a Hobson where the kernel, all views, all libraries, and all user code are written in Hob, with the interpreter itself being the only JavaScript item. The development experience aspires to Smalltalk: a live browser where you navigate items, see their structure, click through references, modify code, and watch changes propagate instantly.

    val forms))

The library's interpreter instance is created, runs, produces exports, and is discarded. The exported functions (closures over their Hob environment) survive as cached JS values. This is exactly how JS modules work too — evaluate once, cache the exports, discard the source context.

The eval loop is async JavaScript internally, so individual Hob expressions are naturally sequential. However, many Hobson operations (item fetches, queries) are I/O-bound, and running them sequentially is unnecessarily slow. Hob provides concurrency at two levels.
bindings for data dependencies. If a binding does not reference any name defined earlier in the same
block, it is independent and can be evaluated concurrently with other independent bindings. This is a compile-time analysis — the evaluator scans each binding's AST for references to earlier names.

(let [notes (find-items {:type @note-type})
      tags  (find-items {:type @tag-type})]
  ...)

;; 'y' depends on 'x' → evaluated sequentially
(let [x (get-item id)
      y (. x :title)]
  ...)

(plet [a (get-item id1)
       b (get-item id2)
       c (get-item id3)]
  (process a b c))

;; pmap — like map but evaluates the function on all elements concurrently

The async/await evaluator has a fundamental limitation: CPU-intensive Hob computations (large maps, complex view trees) block the JavaScript thread until the next I/O await point, freezing the UI. A continuation-passing style (CPS) evaluator would solve this by making every evaluation step suspendable. The interpreter could yield after N steps, check for pending user input, and resume — like React's fiber architecture. CPS also enables cooperative concurrency (interleaving multiple computations), cancellation, and time-budgeted evaluation. This is the right long-term architecture for a Smalltalk-inspired live environment, but adds roughly 2x implementation complexity compared to async/await. Defer until there's concrete evidence of UI responsiveness problems (likely Phase 4+).

Hob vectors are JavaScript arrays. Hob maps are plain JavaScript objects. This makes FFI zero-cost (no marshaling) at the expense of Hob data being mutable from JavaScript. Acceptable tradeoff for a single-user system.

Watches (Phase 4) are simpler than reactivity (Phase 5) and deliver visible value immediately (logging, indexing, event handling). Reactivity requires careful engineering around dependency tracking and cleanup. Building watches first lets views work with explicit event handling, providing a working baseline before adding automatic reactivity.
No phase depends on future phases for usefulness. Phase 1 is a better REPL. Phase 3 is a better way to write views. Each is worth doing even if you stop there.
Hob supplements JavaScript; it doesn't replace it by force. Any item can use JavaScript. Migration is gradual and voluntary. There is never a moment where existing JavaScript code stops working.

Hob should be the obvious choice for any user-programming within Hobson. There should be no reason to choose JS except for familiarity. Hob — and the way it integrates with Hobson — should be better than JS for most things, and as good for the rest.

This is not "Hob is a nice option" or "Hob works for simple views." It's a stronger claim: a Hobson user who knows both JS and Hob should reach for Hob every time, because Hob understands Hobson in ways that JS never can.
Why Hob can be better than JS
Hob's advantage is not that it's a better general-purpose language — it isn't, and doesn't need to be. Its advantage is that it's a
language. Hobson concepts are Hob concepts:
is a reference to an item, not a string constant you look up.
are language-level operations, not API calls.
With JSON AST as canonical representation (see
), Hob code is stored in the same format as everything else in Hobson. It's queryable, transformable, and inspectable with the same tools as any item property.
Because Hob code runs through an evaluator (not
), the system can sandbox it, track its dependencies, inspect its state, and assist meaningfully. JS is opaque; Hob is transparent.
Users can define new syntactic patterns that operate on code structure. This is impossible in JS without a build system.
Enabled by code-as-data. Edit code structure directly, no syntax errors possible. The editor understands what you're editing because the code is structured data, not text.
is the escape hatch, not the goal
provides general JS interop — call any JS function, access any API. It's necessary but should feel like reaching for a screwdriver when the toolbox is right there. If a Hob view is mostly

name: Rendering Architecture Review: Reactivity and the Spatial Canvas Question

description.s: With the nested rendering fix complete (

), spatial-canvas-view conversion to Hob is technically unblocked. Before committing to that, this review examines whether spatial-canvas is the right next step, or whether foundational work in the rendering stack would be more valuable first.
The end goal is a simple and robust reactive rendering approach for Hob views. JS view compatibility can be dropped if it simplifies the design.
How the Rendering Stack Works Today
Three layers combine to implement rendering:
(f1111111-0002) is a stateless library (~269 lines) that determines
to render. URL is authoritative for the root item ID. The viewport item (
) stores the view config (which view to use, layout state).
updates URL + viewport item + triggers re-render via the rendering system.
(33333333-5555) is the largest component (~1077 lines). It determines
: preference hierarchy (explicit viewId > item.preferredView > type.preferredView > type chain > default-view)
): tracks every rendered DOM node by itemId, viewId, parentId, trackingId
: ITEM_UPDATED / ITEM_DELETED events + atom mutations > DependencyTracker lookup > microtask-batched re-renders
: defined in the Hob interpreter (40b00001) but initialized and driven by the rendering system
(ef793c27, ~617 lines JS + 5 libraries ~500 lines): manages window chrome (drag, resize, z-index, minimize, anchor/dock), delegates content to
: evaluate Hob code, return hiccup, converted to DOM via
> Each child gets its own render instance + tracking context (the nested rendering fix)
> Later: item changes > ITEM_UPDATED > dep tracker finds dependents > schedule re-render
> For Hob views: full re-eval + morphdom patch; for JS views: full re-eval + replaceChild
remain (13 are 3-4 line wrappers delegating to generic-view)
: type-workshop-view (751 lines), spatial-canvas-view (618 lines + 5 libs), app-page-view (378 lines), test-suite-view (296 lines)
1. Dual rendering paths (JS vs Hob) — multiplicative complexity
flag on DOM nodes is a runtime type tag that selects between these paths.
is ~200 lines of branching because of this duality.
2. Whole-view reactivity is too coarse for complex views
The reactive unit is the entire view. Any dependency change triggers full re-evaluation of the entire Hob program, construction of a complete new DOM tree, and morphdom diffing against the old tree.

For a 10-element note view, this is fine. For spatial-canvas with 20 windows, this means re-evaluating all 20 windows' chrome code when one window moves, creating ~200 new DOM elements, and morphdom diffing all of them — only to discover that one element's
The current JS spatial-canvas avoids this with

: drag handlers update CSS directly, then do a "silent update" (persist to DB without re-rendering). Converting to Hob without addressing this means either accepting the performance hit or reimplementing the same workaround — which undermines the reactive model.
3. No independent reactive scope within a view
creates independent reactive scopes, but only for items. There's no way to create an independent reactive scope for a subpart of a view that isn't backed by a separate item.

Spatial-canvas needs each window chrome to be independently reactive. Currently impossible without making each window chrome its own item (conceptually wrong) or using direct DOM mutation (breaks the reactive model).
The DependencyTracker already supports nested contexts via the
chain. The mechanism exists; it's just only accessible through

Defined in the Hob interpreter (40b00001) but used by the rendering system for both JS and Hob views. The rendering system lazy-loads it from the Hob module. This means the rendering system needs the Hob language loaded to do any dependency tracking.
event handler transfer. All exist because cleanup must survive morphdom patching.
This is the deepest issue. The rendering system hardcodes

, so every view depends on its own item. For spatial-canvas, the parent view depends on the parent item. When any attachment's metadata changes (z-index, position), the parent item changes, and the parent view re-renders.

Even with independent child scopes (components), the parent re-renders. If child scopes are eagerly evaluated (as normal function calls would be), the parent re-render creates and then discards 20 child instances — all wasted work.
This means any fine-grained reactivity approach must address how the parent avoids doing wasted work when re-rendering.
to Hob. Parent produces lightweight descriptors (not evaluated DOM). Rendering system reconciles by key: existing components are skipped, new ones are mounted, removed ones are cleaned up.

;; Calling (window-chrome "abc" "xyz") returns a descriptor, not DOM
[:__component {:key "abc" :impl window-chrome-impl :args ["abc" "xyz"]}]
recognizes component descriptors: if a matching instance exists (by key), returns the existing DOM node; otherwise evaluates the component.
(+) General-purpose, proven model, handles all cases
(+) Parent re-render is cheap (produces descriptors, no child evaluation)
(-) Changes Hob evaluation semantics — a component call doesn't execute its body (surprising in a Lisp)
(-) Requires key-based identity for components in loops

(+) Zero new primitives, works with existing

(-) Proliferates items (one placement per window per canvas)

Fundamentally different rendering model. The view function runs
to set up a reactive graph. DOM nodes update directly when signal dependencies change. No re-evaluation, no morphdom.

(defn window-chrome [parent-id child-id]
  (let [att (derive (fn [] (find-attachment (get-item parent-id) child-id)))]
    ;; style.left updates directly when att changes
    ;; No view re-render, no hiccup, no morphdom
    [:div.window {:style {:left (str (:x (deref att)) "px")}}
      (render-item child-id)]))
(+) Maximum efficiency — surgical DOM updates, zero wasted work
(+) Eliminates morphdom entirely (and all its complexity: event handler transfer, input preservation, nested instance skipping)
(+) Arguably most Lisp-natural — expressions describe reactive relationships, not render snapshots
(-) Biggest departure from current model — complete paradigm shift
(-) Hiccup becomes a reactive template, not a pure data structure
(-) Can't mix with current "eval > hiccup > morphdom" approach without two rendering models coexisting
(-) Harder to debug — the view function ran once, possibly long ago
(-) Every piece of reactive data needs to be wrapped in a signal/derive
to not require an item. A
creates an independent reactive scope parameterized by a selector function:

(defn spatial-canvas [item]
  [:div.canvas
    (for [child-id (map :id (:attachments item))]
      (render-view
        ;; Selector: re-runs when deps change, scope only re-renders when result changes
        (fn [] (find-attachment (get-item (:id item)) child-id))
        ;; View: receives selector result
        (fn [att-data]
          [:div.window {:style (pos-style att-data)}
            (render-item child-id)])))])
On parent item change: selectors re-run (cheap array lookup). Only changed scopes re-render.
(+) Explicit selector makes reactivity boundaries visible
(+) Separates "what data do I need" from "how do I render it"
(-) Still needs lazy evaluation (same reconciliation machinery as Alt 1)
(-) Two functions per scope (selector + view) — more boilerplate
(-) Converges with Alt 1 in implementation; different mainly in ergonomics

ITEM_UPDATED events already contain both the previous and current item data. Currently the rendering system ignores this — it just extracts the item ID and schedules re-renders for all dependents. This alternative uses that diff information to filter at the scheduling stage: scopes register a
function when they record a dependency, and the rendering system only schedules a re-render when the selector returns a different value for old vs new.

;; Parent view registers: "I only care about which children exist"
(watch-item! (:id item)
  :select (fn [item] (map :id (:attachments item))))

;; Window-chrome scope registers: "I only care about my specific attachment entry"
(watch-item! parent-id
  :select (fn [item] (find-attachment item child-id)))
When a z-index changes on one window:
ITEM_UPDATED fires with previous + current parent item
20 window-chrome selectors: 19 return identical attachment entries —
Total: 1 re-render of 1 window-chrome scope. Zero wasted work.
This dissolves the parent re-render problem without lazy evaluation.

The parent never re-renders for position/z-index/minimize changes because its selector filters them out. Since the parent doesn't re-render, it doesn't eagerly evaluate child scopes, so the lazy evaluation problem from Alt 1 simply doesn't arise. For structural changes (add/remove window — rare), the parent's selector detects a difference in the child ID list and re-renders normally.
Implementation is a contained change to existing infrastructure:
a scope re-renders, but you still need a mechanism to define
constitutes a scope. The key insight is that the scoping mechanism can be much simpler than in Alt 1 — no lazy evaluation, no reconciliation, no keying. Simple eager components or
calls suffice, because selectors prevent the parent from re-rendering in the common case.
(+) Small, contained infrastructure change — selector registry + scheduling filter
(+) Dissolves the parent re-render problem for the common case (data changes) without lazy evaluation
(+) Backward compatible — scopes without selectors re-render on any change (current behavior)
(+) Works with any scoping mechanism (components, render-view, even plain render-item)
(+) Selectors are explicit and inspectable — easy to debug reactivity
(+) Uses information (the diff) that already exists but is currently discarded
(-) Still needs some form of independent scope for window chromes (not a complete solution alone)
(-) Selector functions run on every ITEM_UPDATED for every dependent — N selectors per item change (though each is cheap)
(-) Structural changes (add/remove) still cause full parent re-render (acceptable if rare)
Alternative 6: Do Nothing — Current Primitives Pragmatically
Convert spatial-canvas to Hob as-is. Use atoms for transient state during drag. Use
for direct DOM mutation at 60fps. Let full morphdom happen on structural changes. Accept the cost.
(+) 20-window morphdom on ~200 elements might actually be fast enough
, direct DOM mutation) make Hob code look like JS with extra syntax
(-) Sets precedent of working around the reactive model
(-) If it IS too slow, we've built on a foundation that needs replacing

Regardless of architecture, continuous 60fps drag requires direct DOM mutation. You can't round-trip through DB + re-eval at 60 times per second. The question is only what happens on mouseup (persist final position) — and whether that triggers a cheap targeted update or an expensive full re-render.
Discrete interactions (click to front, minimize) are the real test

These are the interactions where reactivity should "just work" without escape hatches. If clicking a window to bring it to front requires a silent update or direct DOM mutation, the reactive model has failed.
With components/derived scopes: update parent item > parent doesn't re-eval (lazy) > only the clicked window's scope re-renders (cheap). Reactivity works naturally.
Without components: update parent item > full canvas re-eval > full morphdom. Works but wasteful. Silent update avoids this but breaks the reactive model.
The parent re-render problem is fundamental

Every approach except Alt 2 (data restructuring), Alt 3 (signals), and Alt 5 (selectors) must contend with the parent re-rendering when any attachment metadata changes. Alt 1 solves this with lazy evaluation. Alt 5 solves it by filtering at the scheduling stage — the parent simply never re-renders for data-only changes. Alt 6 accepts it. This problem shapes the design more than any other factor.
Item-level dependency tracking is the root cause — but selectors may be enough

The current system tracks dependencies at item granularity: "this context depends on item X." When item X changes in any way, all dependents re-render. Full path-level tracking ("this context depends on item X's attachments[3].z") would solve this but is a significant infrastructure change requiring proxy objects or similar.

However, selector-filtered scheduling (Alt 5) achieves a similar practical result with much less machinery. Rather than tracking which paths are accessed, each scope declares what slice of the item it cares about. The rendering system compares that slice between old and new item on every update. This is coarser than true path-level tracking but sufficient for the known use cases, and the implementation is straightforward.

is the most promising near-term approach. It's a small, contained change to existing infrastructure that dissolves the parent re-render problem for the common case. It needs to be paired with a scoping mechanism (independent reactive scopes for window chromes), but that mechanism can be simple — no lazy evaluation, no reconciliation. Selectors handle the hard part (when to re-render), leaving the scoping mechanism to handle the easy part (what to re-render).

is the best long-term architecture but the biggest rewrite. It eliminates morphdom entirely, removing a huge source of complexity. Worth considering whether selectors are a stepping stone toward signals or an alternative path.
is worth trying first as a measurement baseline. We don't actually know that 20-window morphdom is too slow.

converge on the same machinery (lazy descriptors + reconciliation) with different ergonomics. Selectors (Alt 5) may make these unnecessary — if the parent doesn't re-render in the common case, lazy evaluation is not needed.
(placement items) is interesting as a data-modeling question independent of rendering architecture.

If we add fine-grained reactivity, should it be the only model (replace whole-view reactivity) or coexist with it?
Could signals and hiccup coexist — e.g., hiccup for static structure, signals for dynamic parts?
Is the dual JS/Hob rendering path worth maintaining, or should we commit to Hob-only and take the conversion hit?
Should DependencyTracker move regardless of which alternative we choose?

For selectors (Alt 5): what equality semantics? Deep structural equality is correct but potentially expensive. Could use a user-provided comparator, or hash-based comparison, or reference equality with immutable data.
For selectors + scopes: what's the simplest scoping mechanism that works? Could

machinery, parameterized by a selector + render function instead of an item ID?
Are selectors a stepping stone toward signals, or an alternative path? Could you start with selectors + morphdom and migrate to signals later without breaking views?

name: Architecture Proposal: Minimal Kernel & Hob Runtime

description.s: Architecture Proposal: Minimal Kernel & Hob Runtime

This proposal restructures Hobson into three clean layers: a minimal JS kernel providing only storage, modules, and events; the Hob interpreter as the system's programming model; and everything else — rendering, navigation, selection, error handling, UI — written in Hob. The goal is a system that describes itself in its own language, where dependencies are explicit and structurally visible, and where the maximum amount of code is inspectable and modifiable from within the system.
The current architecture has evolved organically. kernel-core is ~2500 lines containing the EventBus, the Kernel class, a ~750-line

method, import/export logic, UI fallbacks (item palette, help dialog, raw editor), and declarative watch dispatch. The rendering system is another ~1100 lines inside the kernel. The kernel hardcodes knowledge of specific userland libraries (viewport-manager, selection-manager) by name.

Meanwhile, Hob — the system's own language — is used only for views. System-level libraries (viewport-manager, selection-manager, keyboard-shortcuts, repl-ui, error handling, etc.) are all raw JS. This means the most architecturally significant code in the system is the least inspectable.
The proposal addresses both problems: shrink the kernel to its irreducible core, and use Hob for everything above it.
The kernel provides the minimum needed to make items-with-dependencies work. Nothing more.
— CRUD operations on items. Type-chain validation. Cycle detection. Owns IndexedDB access and ID prefixing for nested instances.

bindings as a map. Cache management and invalidation on code item changes.

field, dispatching events to matching handlers). This is the mechanism through which userland activates at boot.
— Initialize storage, ensure seed items, build event type cache, setup watches, emit

— The kernel provides a bare-bones REPL (eval input, show output) as part of its fallback state. This is distinct from the full-featured REPL (syntax highlighting, history, autocomplete, UI chrome) which is a Layer 3 service. The kernel REPL is deliberately minimal — just enough to inspect items, evaluate expressions, and recover from a broken Layer 3.
— Catch uncaught errors and promise rejections, emit
events. The kernel does not handle errors itself (no toast, no error items) — it just emits the event. A userland watcher handles the rest.
. That's the complete surface. No rendering, no navigation, no viewport, no attach/detach, no import/export.
Layer 2: Hob (JS interpreter, first thing loaded)
The Hob interpreter is necessarily JS — it can't be written in the language it interprets. But it's the only JS at this level. Everything above it is Hob.
Hob's role is not just "view language" but "the system's programming model." It provides:

— Code remains as AST throughout its lifecycle. Before require, it's an AST in storage. After require, the interpreter has evaluated it, but the AST is still there in the item. Nothing is compiled away or hidden.
— Atoms with automatic dependency tracking. When an atom mutates, the system knows which rendered contexts depend on it and can re-render them.
— Declarative DOM construction from data structures.

calls), item references, and more — without executing the code. Tooling written in Hob can operate on Hob.

— The interpreter is the single point of failure for all of Layer 3. If it fails to load or throws during evaluation, the kernel falls back to JS-based raw views for the broken items and the safe mode REPL. This keeps the system recoverable without requiring the interpreter to be perfect, and allows the interpreter to be iterated on aggressively.
All system-level concerns become Hob modules, orchestrated by the viewport manager.

The system's dependency graph, event flow, and module structure are all visible as data. A system browser can walk Hob ASTs to show what requires what, what subscribes to which events, what types a view handles. No string parsing, no heuristics — structural queries on structured data.

Today, kernel-core is an opaque 95KB blob. The rendering system is 40KB of opaque JS. In this model, the kernel shrinks to ~1000 lines of truly irreducible infrastructure, and everything else is inspectable Hob that the user can open, read, understand, and modify.

Today, system-level libraries are JS with ad-hoc patterns. Views are Hob with reactive state. Watchers are JS with convention-based handler names. In this model, everything speaks the same language with the same patterns for state (atoms), dependencies (require), and lifecycle (watches).
. But the dependency is right there. You can see it. The system can see it. There's no magic global, no kernel method hiding where the call actually goes.
Currently kernel methods. But the kernel doesn't traverse or interpret the attachment graph for its own purposes — rendering does. These methods are sugar over

— Loads the Hob interpreter (its dependency), renders the root item

If step 4 or 5 fails (broken viewport or rendering code), the kernel's DOM root shows its safe mode state: the basic REPL and raw JSON display. The user can fix things via that REPL or safe mode (Ctrl+Shift+S).
This is a significant restructuring. A staged approach:
Extract import/export, raw editor, item palette fallback, and help dialog fallback out of kernel-core into separate items. Remove hardcoded
to pure kernel primitives. This can be done independently and tested against existing userland.
Extend the module system so that requiring a Hob item evaluates its AST in a child environment and returns local bindings as a map. This is the foundational capability for Hob modules.
Stage 3: Move rendering out of the kernel.

The rendering system becomes a Hob module (or a set of Hob modules) required by the viewport manager. This interleaves with the nested rendering work — the new rendering approach would be built outside the kernel from the start.
Stage 4: Port JS libraries to Hob.

Starting with simpler ones (selection-manager, keyboard-shortcuts) and working up to viewport-manager and repl-ui. Each port is independent and testable. Profile hot-path performance before committing — keyboard dispatch and selection tracking need sub-frame response times. Some services may need to remain JS if async overhead is prohibitive.

As functionality moves to Hob, the kernel shrinks. Eventually kernel-core is just: boot sequence, storage composition, module system composition, event bus, watch dispatch, safe mode REPL, and a minimal base API.

The interpreter is currently fast enough for views. Will it be fast enough for system-level code that runs on every event? The async-everything nature of Hob (every function returns a Promise) is the real constraint. Keyboard shortcut dispatch, selection management, and event routing are hot paths that run synchronously on every interaction. The interop pitfalls already known (Hob fns can't be used as synchronous callbacks) would apply to these system-level services too. Profiling is needed before committing to porting hot-path libraries. Some services may need to stay JS, or Hob may need a synchronous evaluation mode.
Some things may always need to be JS (e.g., interfacing with CodeMirror, markdown parsers, other JS libraries loaded from CDN). Hob already has
for calling JS methods on objects. The question is whether Hob modules can cleanly wrap JS libraries, or whether some items need to remain JS.

At ~3200 lines and 109KB, the interpreter is the largest single item. It's necessarily JS. Under this proposal it becomes the single point of failure for all of Layer 3 — a bug that currently breaks only views would now break the entire system. The JS view fallback path and safe mode REPL mitigate this, but the interpreter's reliability and debuggability matter more in this architecture. Should it remain a single monolithic item, or be decomposed?

After bulk-migrating item descriptions from markdown strings to
ASTs, startup went from near-instant to ~4 s and Ctrl+K became unusably slow. This documents the root causes and fixes.
Root cause: Hob interpreter overhead on structural data

The core issue was not data size (ASTs are only ~1.6× larger than equivalent markdown). It was that code paths which previously touched a single string per item were now recursively walking deeply nested arrays — and some of that recursion ran inside the Hob interpreter rather than native JS.

The Hob interpreter is not suitable for tight recursive data processing. Any function that walks a tree of arbitrary depth — text extraction, link scanning, serialization — must be implemented in JS and exposed as a stdlib function. The interpreter is for view logic and orchestration, not data crunching. This applies doubly when the function runs per-item in a list (O(items × AST_depth) interpreter calls).

More broadly: when migrating data formats, audit every code path that touches the changed fields — not just the ones that read/write them, but the ones that incidentally process them (search indexing, link extraction, preview generation, rendering). The regression was not in the Active Text renderer itself but in peripheral code that assumed string descriptions.

Hob Expressions as Universal Query Language
Today the system uses several special-purpose representations for "describe a computation over items":
— a custom string syntax with ad-hoc parsing
— the same JS objects passed to

These are all the same operation (filter items by criteria) expressed in three different ways, none of which can be inspected, composed, or reused across contexts. The search syntax is exactly the kind of mini-language the design doc argues against.
Predicates as the Universal Query Mechanism

In most languages, there is a tension between declarative queries (inspectable but limited) and procedural predicates (flexible but opaque). In Hob, this tension does not exist. Hob expressions are data — an AST that can be walked, displayed, and edited. A predicate function is already a declarative representation. There is no need for a separate query DSL.

AST is a Hob expression at block position that returns AST data. The renderer evaluates it and renders the result:

(let [modules (sort-by :name
                (filter (fn [m] (type? m @kernel-module))
                  (get-all)))]
  [:ul
    (map (fn [m]
      [:li [:p
        [:item-ref (:id m) (:name m)]
        {s: " — "}
        {s: (or (first (str/split (or (get-in m [:content :description]) "") "\n"))
                "No description")}]])
      modules)])
This replaces the current JS query blocks. The expression is inspectable — the editor can display it, and "Explain this" can trace its evaluation.

Because inline content is a flat list (not a recursive tree), the inline editing problem is tractable — it is sequence manipulation, not tree manipulation.

Automerge is not the right approach for Hobson. The impedance mismatch between Automerge's operation-level model and Hobson's snapshot-based API creates permanent complexity (diffing layer, map key ordering, bootstrap chicken-and-egg) that outweighs the benefits. A simpler design based on snapshot history + nested instance promotion was chosen instead. See
Investigate whether Automerge is the right storage foundation for Hobson's next phase: system-level undo + mobile sync.
Two upcoming needs converge on the same problem:
Deleting an item, removing an attachment, changing a type are all irreversible. The system needs a way to revert destructive operations.
Hobson needs to be accessible on mobile, which requires syncing data between devices with conflict resolution.
Automerge is a CRDT library that potentially solves both: its operation log gives history/undo, and its CRDT foundation enables sync with automatic conflict resolution.
Automerge lives in the kernel storage layer. The rest of Hobson does not interact with Automerge directly.

A.load(bytes) → Automerge doc → convert to plain JS object → return to caller. Callers receive a mutable plain object, never an Automerge proxy. This is functionally necessary because callers mutate the returned object before passing it back to api.set().

Caller passes a plain JS object (as today) → storage layer diffs it against the current Automerge doc → applies minimal A.change() mutations at field level (not character level) → A.save() → bytes to IDB. This preserves the existing api.set(item) interface.
History/revert belongs in the kernel storage layer, not as a userland item — item edits must not be able to break the history mechanism. The storage API would expose:
— list of changes with timestamps and messages
— read-only plain object at a historical state (uses A.view(), which is cheap)
— reverts item to a previous state by diffing and applying reverse patches
A userland history-view can call these APIs for the UI, but the mechanism itself is protected in the kernel.

Automerge has no cross-document query mechanism. Hobson already maintains indexes in related-items-lib. The existing query/search pattern (load items, filter in JS) continues to work. A lightweight metadata index could avoid deserialising full items for bulk queries.

api.get() returns a plain object clone (JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(doc))). This is sub-millisecond per item, but getAll() on 337+ items needs benchmarking. Alternative: return Automerge proxies directly for reads, clone only when caller needs mutability. Needs prototyping to see what breaks.

The storage layer must diff a plain JS object against an Automerge doc to produce fine-grained A.change() mutations. Object/primitive fields are straightforward. Arrays (tags, attachments, Active Text ASTs) need a diffing strategy — element-by-element comparison with fallback to full replacement. Needs prototyping.
Automerge stores full operation history. For Hobson's whole-field-value pattern, overhead is estimated at 2-3x raw JSON. Need to measure on real items.
Automerge's core is Rust compiled to WASM. Adds to initial load time and requires async initialisation. Need to measure impact on boot.

Reverting a field change is straightforward (diff + reverse patches). But reverting item deletion means the item's Automerge doc must still exist somewhere. May need soft-delete (mark as deleted, keep the doc) rather than actual removal.

What does mobile sync look like? automerge-repo handles document lifecycle and sync adapters. A sync server (or peer-to-peer via WebRTC) is needed. This is a later concern but the storage layer should not preclude it.

PouchDB was considered but its revision system discards old bodies on compaction — designed for sync conflict resolution, not version history. Yjs is another CRDT option but has a different storage model. A custom IDB history store (copy-on-write) is simpler but doesn't help with sync.
Before committing to Automerge, build a minimal prototype to get hard numbers:
Take a representative large item (view with hundreds of lines of code, doc with a big Active Text AST).
Create an Automerge doc from it. Measure A.from() and A.save() sizes.
Measure JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(doc)) conversion time, singly and in bulk (337x).
Implement a naive field-level diff (old doc vs new plain object). Measure diffing + A.change() time.
Test Active Text AST mutations: insert block, change block type, edit text. Verify Automerge handles the nested structure correctly.
Measure A.getHistory(), A.view(), and A.diff() on a doc with ~50 changes.

If the prototype shows acceptable performance, proceed with integrating Automerge into the kernel storage layer. If not, evaluate whether proxy-based reads (skipping conversion) or a simpler custom approach is needed.

Automerge 3.2.4, Firefox, standalone HTML harness (perf/automerge-bench.html). Write/history numbers from spatial-canvas-view (52.5KB, largest item). A.load() scaling tested across five items from 1.3KB to 52.5KB.

Scaling is linear with document size — no significant fixed per-document overhead.

281ms. Only needed for one-time migration, not ongoing operation.

All metrics are acceptable. A.load() is the only concern, but full boot simulation across all 337 real items shows 1.49s total — dominated by a handful of large library items. Storage is a net win: Automerge binary is 39% smaller than JSON (2.34 MB vs 3.82 MB). With lazy loading, perceived boot cost would be well under 200ms.
