A lightweight IDB store with (id, name, type, tags) for each item, updated on every write. Avoids deserializing all Automerge docs for search/listing. Bulk queries hit the index; full docs loaded on-demand.
Move A.load() to a Web Worker so background loading doesn't block the main thread.
If lazy loading proves insufficient, store both JSON (for fast reads) and Automerge binary (for history/sync) in IDB. Adds write-path complexity but preserves current boot speed exactly.
Automerge supports maps, lists, text (with rich-text marks), strings, booleans, null, integers, floats, counters, timestamps, bytes — a superset of JSON.
Documents read like plain JS objects (proxy-based). JSON.stringify() works directly.
Documents are immutable outside of A.change() — callers need a mutable clone, which is why the plain-object conversion on read is functionally necessary.
Active Text ASTs (nested arrays of mixed types) work natively. Fine-grained mutations on nested elements are supported. Replacing whole subtrees works but loses merge granularity.
A.view(doc, oldHeads) gives cheap read-only snapshots at any historical state (shares memory, no copying). A.diff() returns structured patches.
No built-in undo — implemented via patch inversion (capture reverse patches during A.change(), apply them to revert).
Storage: A.save() produces compact binary (Uint8Array) for IDB. A.load() restores. No need for automerge-repo for basic persistence.
Automerge 3.0 has 10x memory improvement over 2.0. Plain strings are collaborative by default; use A.ImmutableString for atomic strings (GUIDs, type IDs).
PouchDB was considered but rejected — its revision system discards old bodies on compaction, making it unsuitable for version history.

A library item wraps the Claude API (fetch to api.anthropic.com with tool use). Tools map directly to Hobson's API. Conversations are items. Any view or REPL command can invoke Claude.
Zero extra processes. AI is a native capability within the item system.

API key stored in the browser.
Option B: Claude Code via MCP

Hobson exposes its API as an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server. Claude Code connects as a client and can call tools natively. This means the same Claude the user is already talking to can reach directly into the running system.
One Claude for everything — development and live changes.
MCP is a standard protocol. Claude Code already supports it natively.
Browsers cannot expose stdio or listen on ports. Requires either a small bridge process or a Tauri shell.
One Claude (Code) that reaches into Hobson via MCP. The transport problem has two solutions depending on Hobson's runtime:

A small (~50 line) Node script translates between MCP stdio and a WebSocket connected to Hobson in the browser. The bridge is stateless plumbing with no application logic. A Hobson library item (mcp-server-lib) opens the WebSocket listener and handles incoming tool calls by dispatching to Hobson's API.

If Hobson moves to a Tauri desktop shell, the transport layer (stdio or local HTTP/SSE) lives in Tauri's Rust backend (~100 lines, built once, never changes). The MCP tool logic lives in a standard Hobson item that receives messages via Tauri's IPC bridge. Claude Code connects via SSE to the Tauri app — no separate process needed.
The tools are thin wrappers around Hobson's existing API:
is the escape hatch — anything without a dedicated tool can be done via eval.
enables Claude to see rendered output (including code that executes during rendering) by capturing a screenshot and returning it as an image for Claude's vision capabilities.
Items can contain code that executes during rendering — Claude needs to see the rendered result, not just the raw JSON. The render_item tool:
Renders the item into a container using Hobson's existing viewport rendering pipeline.
Waits for render to settle (async code, network loads, etc.).
Captures the container via html2canvas (loaded as a Hobson library item) → base64 PNG.
Returns the image to Claude, who can assess it via vision.
This closes the feedback loop: Claude makes a change, sees the rendered result, and can self-correct — all within a single conversation turn.

The bridge process violates the 'no extra processes' constraint but is trivial. Tauri eliminates it but is a larger commitment. Does Hobson move to Tauri for other reasons (filesystem access, offline, system integration) that make this a natural step?
For Option A (in-browser), the key lives in a Hobson item or config. For Option B (Claude Code), Claude Code manages its own key. If both are eventually needed, key storage should be unified.
Should Claude always execute changes immediately, or show a preview for code changes? This is a policy choice that can be tuned later, but the tool schema should support both modes.

How much of Hobson's state should Claude see in each conversation? All items? Just the relevant ones? The tool-use approach naturally scopes this — Claude fetches what it needs — but system prompt context matters too.
Claude Code builds the MCP integration, but once built, it largely replaces the file-editing workflow. How does Claude Code fix the MCP integration itself if it breaks?

Hobson runs in a browser today. This doc maps platform capabilities across browser-only, desktop shell, mobile shell, and hard limits. The chosen direction is all-Tauri (desktop + Android mobile) with Automerge running as native Rust in the Tauri backend. See the Chosen Direction section for implementation order.

The web platform is surprisingly capable. You have Canvas, WebGL, WebGPU, IndexedDB, OPFS, Web Workers, WASM, WebRTC, audio/video capture, and service workers (if served from localhost). This is enough for rich editors, knowledge tools, drawing apps, visualizations, games, data analysis, peer-to-peer collaboration, and local-first databases.
Git clients, file managers, "save to ~/Documents". The File System Access API exists (Chromium-only) but requires a user gesture each session and can't watch for changes.
SSH clients, direct database connections (Postgres, Redis), IMAP/SMTP email, custom protocol implementations. You're limited to HTTP(S), WebSocket, and WebRTC.
Terminal emulators, build systems, running scripts, automating other apps.
Can't listen on ports. Can't serve files to other devices on your LAN.
No global hotkeys, system tray, file-type associations, "open with Hobson", or persistent native notifications.
Browser can suspend/kill tabs and service workers. No reliable cron, no file watcher, no daemon behavior.
Can't talk to arbitrary APIs unless they opt in. This kills a large category of integrations.

protocol is even more restricted: no service workers, no secure-context APIs (Web Serial, WebBluetooth, WebUSB, credential management), and stricter CORS. Serving from localhost is the minimum viable choice for serious use.
A desktop shell removes nearly every browser sandbox constraint. The webview remains the rendering engine, but you gain a backend with full OS access.
Read/write/watch anywhere. Git clients, file managers, backup systems, import/export anything.
Terminal emulators, build tools, shell scripts, launching other apps.
TCP/UDP sockets for SSH, database drivers, SMTP/IMAP, custom protocols.
Other apps and devices can talk to Hobson. Local API server, LAN sync.
System tray, global hotkeys, deep links, file associations, native menus, auto-launch on boot.
Proxy any request through the backend. Every API is reachable.

Spawn llama.cpp, whisper.cpp, or any inference engine as child processes.
SQLite on disk, or connect directly to Postgres, Redis, etc.

Tauri (Rust backend) gives a smaller binary, better security model, and an explicit API surface. Critically, it shares a Rust backend between desktop and mobile, enabling a single codebase for all platform capabilities. Automerge (also written in Rust) runs natively in the backend with no WASM layer.

A desktop shell transforms Hobson from "an app you use in a browser" into "a platform that can host other apps." It could become your terminal, your file manager, your email client, your IDE — all as items.

Tauri Mobile wraps a webview in a native Android shell. The same Rust backend used on desktop compiles to Android, sharing all platform capability code including Automerge storage. iOS is not a target.
What Mobile Shells Still Can't Do
— require native Kotlin, not webview content
— HealthKit/Health Connect need native entitlements and review
— webview has inherent overhead vs native UI for complex touch interactions

One Rust backend compiles to desktop (Linux, macOS, Windows) and mobile (Android). Platform-specific capabilities are exposed to the webview via Tauri's IPC bridge and surfaced as Hobson items or libraries. The item model doesn't change — only the API surface underneath grows. Automerge storage, sync, and MCP server all live in the shared Rust backend.
The capability space is a matrix, not a ladder:

Desktop              Mobile
                -------              ------
Current:        Browser (file://)    None
Planned:        Tauri                Tauri Mobile (Android)
Hard limits:    real-time, kernel,   real-time, kernel,
                peak perf            widgets, deep OS integration
Even with native shells on every platform, some things remain structurally impossible:
— JS has a garbage collector, an event loop, and no deterministic scheduling. Medical devices, industrial PLCs, and flight control systems are out.
— Hobson is always a userspace guest. No device drivers, no filesystem implementations, no hypervisors.
— The JS→WASM→WebGPU abstraction layers have real overhead vs native CUDA/Metal/Vulkan. Good performance, not best performance.

— Home screen widgets, voice assistant intents, health/fitness APIs, Instant Apps, and NFC payments require native code that sits outside the webview entirely. A mobile shell gets you most of the way, but not here.
— DRM, secure enclaves, TPM attestation. These require platform-level integration below the application layer.

All-Tauri with native Rust Automerge. One Rust backend shared between desktop and Android, with Automerge running natively (no WASM). The webview renders UI; the backend owns storage, sync, and platform capabilities.
Wrap Hobson in Tauri. Keep IDB storage in the webview initially. Everything works as before, but a Rust backend now exists.
Implement storage with native Automerge, exposed to the webview via Tauri IPC. Replace the IDB storage layer. This gives system-level undo and version history.
The shared Rust backend compiles to Android. Automerge storage and sync come for free.
Automerge's CRDT foundation enables device sync. The Rust backend handles network transport; Automerge handles conflict resolution.

Automerge is written in Rust. Running it as WASM in the webview works (benchmarked in the Automerge Investigation) but adds an unnecessary layer: WASM compilation, WASM init time (4-7.5s from CDN), WASM memory boundary. Since the Tauri backend is already Rust, Automerge runs natively with no overhead. The backend can also directly access items for sync, MCP, and backup without crossing the webview boundary.
The all-Tauri-native direction has real tradeoffs. These concerns don't invalidate the recommendation but should be weighed before committing.
The benchmarks don't measure the proposed architecture

All numbers in the Automerge Investigation were measured with WASM running in-process in the browser. The proposed architecture puts Automerge in a separate Rust backend behind Tauri IPC. Every api.get() and api.set() would cross a serialization boundary (JS → JSON → IPC → Rust → Automerge → Rust → JSON → IPC → JS). The 1.5ms write path and sub-millisecond reads could look different with IPC round-trip overhead, especially for bulk operations. IPC-specific benchmarks are needed before committing.
The “Why Not WASM?” argument overstates the problem

The three stated reasons — WASM compilation, 4–7.5s CDN init, memory boundary — are largely deployment problems, not architectural ones. Compilation is one-time and cached by the browser. Init time is 4–7.5s from CDN; bundled locally inside Tauri it drops dramatically. The WASM memory boundary cost is traded for an IPC boundary cost involving serialization on every call — potentially worse for frequent small operations.

Hobson draws from Smalltalk and Lisp — everything is inspectable and modifiable from inside the system. Moving storage to Rust means the storage layer is no longer accessible from the REPL, no longer modifiable as an item, and no longer written in the language the user works in. This goes beyond the kernel boundary rule: storage moves outside the item system and outside JavaScript entirely.

Step 1 preserves the current single-file-in-a-browser story. Step 2 replaces IDB with native Automerge via IPC, meaning Hobson can only run inside Tauri from that point forward. Maintaining browser fallback would require a dual storage path indefinitely.

A middle path: bundle Automerge WASM locally inside Tauri, keeping storage in the webview. This gives undo/history, fast WASM init (local, not CDN), browser fallback capability, live-inspectable storage, and the Tauri shell for OS capabilities. Sync could work via Automerge's built-in protocol from the webview side. The native Rust path becomes an optimization to defer until IPC benchmarks prove it's worth the tradeoffs.

The browser sandbox is the single biggest constraint. All-Tauri removes it on both desktop and Android with a single shared Rust backend. Automerge in native Rust gives system-level undo, version history, and device sync without a WASM layer. The remaining hard limits (real-time, kernel, peak perf, deepest OS integration) are things almost no personal tool needs.

Deleting an item, removing an attachment, changing a type are all irreversible today. The system needs a way to revert destructive operations.
Replacing git as the versioning mechanism.
Item history should live inside Hobson, not in an external tool. This fits the "everything in Hobson" philosophy and makes history available at runtime — browsable, revertable, and syncable.
Single-user, device-to-device sync. Hobson needs to be accessible on mobile, which requires syncing data between devices.

). The prototype surfaced a fundamental impedance mismatch: Automerge wants fine-grained operations (mutations inside A.change()), but Hobson's API provides coarse-grained snapshots (api.get() → mutate → api.set()). This creates permanent complexity:

The storage module must reverse-engineer intent from snapshot comparisons. This is inherently lossy (array insertions cannot be detected without LCS) and fragile (every new data structure may need diffing fixes). The storage module nearly doubled in size (276 → 506 lines).

Automerge maps are unordered. Any code relying on Object.keys() iteration order breaks. Fixable for top-level item fields, but not for arbitrary nested objects (e.g., view-spec ui_hints) without data model changes in every affected item.
If Automerge is the storage layer, it must be available before the kernel loads, creating a chicken-and-egg problem requiring a BIOS layer or dual IDB stores.

Automerge excels at large text documents with character-level collaborative edits. Hobson items are small structured JSON objects with many fields — CRDT per-field metadata dominates (40x WASM heap ratio).
CRDTs solve concurrent multi-user editing. Hobson is single-user. The actual sync need (device-to-device for one person) is much simpler and doesn't require CRDTs.
IDB object store holds historical snapshots. Each entry is
, where snapshot is the full item state at that point. The store is append-only.

On every saveItem(), before writing the new state to the items store, the previous state is written to item-history. This happens in the kernel write path — it cannot be bypassed or broken by userland code.

Although the ITEM_UPDATED event carries the previous state (so a userland listener could capture it), history is a safety net. It must survive userland failures — a buggy code item must not be able to disable history. It must be available in safe mode. And the kernel already owns IDB.
— returns list of {itemId, timestamp} entries for an item
— returns the full item snapshot at that timestamp
— restores an item to a previous state. Goes through the normal write path (saveItem), so the revert itself is recorded in history.
Initial implementation stores full snapshots. The API returns full item objects regardless of internal representation, so a future migration to diff-based storage is invisible to callers.
Nested instances provide safe isolation for risky changes, especially kernel-level editing. If a change breaks the nested instance, the parent is unaffected — discard and try again.

Promoting a nested instance to its parent is an atomic commit: all changed items are applied to the parent in one operation. This gives Hobson grouped, reviewable changesets without imposing an explicit commit workflow.
A nested instance is created as a full copy of the parent's items. Self-contained, no fallback chain to the parent on reads.
Edit items in the nested instance. The parent is unaffected.
Identify which items in the nested instance differ from their parent counterparts (new, modified, or deleted). The item's modified timestamp gives a fast check, with full comparison as fallback.
Apply changes to the parent. Each promoted item goes through the normal write path (saveItem), so history is captured automatically. All promoted items share a promotion timestamp.
Discard the nested instance after successful promotion.
The nested instance's name/description serves as the commit message.
Single-user sync between devices. No CRDTs needed — concurrent edits to the same item are rare for one person, and when they occur, last-write-wins with a prompt on conflict is sufficient.
Exchange items as JSON over any transport (relay server, WebRTC, shared file).
Compare modified timestamps. Push the newer version. Flag conflicts where both sides modified since last sync.

History entries from item-history sync alongside items. History entries are immutable and append-only, keyed by (itemId, timestamp) — no conflicts possible, just union the sets. This means edits made on device A can be reverted on device B.

Based on the current item set (342 items, 6.6 MB total JSON, ~7000 historical edits across 653 git commits):
~100–200 MB (overestimate; items were smaller in earlier edits)

Well within IDB limits on desktop (10+ GB). Mobile browsers (Safari/iOS) cap at ~1 GB and may evict under storage pressure — monitor in practice. If full-snapshot storage becomes a concern, migrate to diff-based storage behind the same API.

If history lives in Hobson and git is no longer the versioning mechanism, what is the backup? Options: periodic export (backup.json already exists), sync to a second device, or both. Don't remove git as a safety net until one of these is in place.
When an item is deleted, its history entries remain in item-history (append-only store, nothing is ever removed). Undelete could reconstruct from the most recent history entry. Needs API design.
When both devices modified the same item since last sync, how is the conflict presented to the user? Needs design when sync work begins.

The history API returns full snapshots. A useful history viewer needs to show what changed between versions. Structured field-level diffing ("name changed from X to Y, tag Z added") is more useful than raw JSON diff for items. This is a userland concern.

description.s: A 2D spatial windowing environment that renders attachments as draggable, resizable windows. The primary container view for organizing multiple items visually. Position data lives in each child’s
object — single source of truth, no separate layout table.

Single-axis resize on the non-docked edge
Multiple items visible, persistent layout, direct manipulation
Context switching, single focus, no spatial memory
Spatial organization matches how people naturally arrange information. The complexity cost is worth the UX benefit for desktop workflows.
Why Positioned Objects Over Separate Layout?
Position data could live in a separate layout table, but that creates synchronization issues (child removed but layout entry remains). Embedding position in the attachment
object is a single source of truth.
(edge-anchored) modes. Floating covers general use. Pinned keeps reference panels visible during scrolling. Docked creates IDE-like panel layouts. All three use the same
field — null/unset for floating, corner string for pinned, edge string for docked.

Earlier versions read z-indices from both DOM and database, causing divergence and unbounded growth. The current design treats the database as the single source of truth — z-index functions read fresh attachments from the DB, never from DOM queries. This eliminates an entire class of stacking bugs.

The 2D canvas is desktop-focused. Mobile should use a different container view (e.g., linear list with swipe navigation). Different containers for different contexts is simpler than responsive design.

description.s: The REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) is Hobson's interactive JavaScript console for querying, scripting, and extending the system at runtime.
The REPL provides direct access to Hobson's API, letting you:
Query and inspect items in storage
Test code before packaging it as libraries or views
The REPL appears as a collapsible panel at the bottom of the viewport. It persists across page reloads.
object with full access to the system:

// Storage operations                  
await api.get(id)                // Get item by ID
await api.set(item)              // Save item (no re-render)
await api.update(item)           // Save item and re-render
await api.delete(id)             // Delete item
await api.query({ name: 'foo' }) // Find items by properties
await api.getAll()               // Get all items

// Code loading
await api.require('library-name') // Load a library by name

// Navigation
await api.navigate(itemId)        // Navigate to item
await api.navigate(id, { field: 'code', line: 42 }) // With scroll target

// Rendering
await api.renderItem(itemId)      // Render an item to DOM
await api.rerenderItem(itemId)    // Re-render visible instances
await api.getViews(typeId)        // Get available views for type

// Events
api.events.on(eventId, handler)   // Subscribe to events
api.events.emit({ type, content }) // Emit event

// Import/Export
await api.import()                // Import items from JSON file
await api.export()                // Export all items to JSON

const item = await api.helpers.findByName('my-library');
return item;

const views = await api.query({ type: api.IDS.VIEW });
return views.map(v => v.name);
